short: The main rulebook agencies follow when they buy goods and services by contract. It sits at Title 48 of the Code of Federal Regulations.
The defense department's supplement to the FAR: extra rules and clauses that apply only to defense contracts.
GSA's own supplement to the FAR. Since November 3, 2025 it holds the ordering procedures for GSA Schedule contracts.
A numbered update to the FAR. The FAC number on a FAR page shows how current the text is.
The online edition of the Code of Federal Regulations, run by the National Archives and the Government Publishing Office.
The collected, numbered text of federal agencies' regulations, cited as title, then part or section (13 CFR 121.201).
The organised collection of federal statutes, cited by title and section (15 U.S.C. 638).
An act of Congress as enacted, before its text is sorted into the U.S. Code. Cited by Congress and number (Pub. L. 119-83).

term: Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act (Pub. L. 119-83)
short: The April 13, 2026 law that restored SBIR and STTR through September 30, 2031 after a six-month lapse, with proposal limits and a security-risk review.
The government's official journal of proposed rules, final rules, notices and executive orders, cited by volume and page (91 FR 51568).
A draft regulation published for public comment. It changes nothing until a final rule follows.
A regulation published in its adopted form, with an effective date after which it binds.
An agency's written authority for its contracting officers to follow text that departs from the codified regulation.
The rewrite of the FAR ordered in April 2025. In force by class deviation; proposed rules issued in 2026; nothing final as of October 3, 2026.
The rule that FAR sections not required by statute expire after four years unless renewed. The official texts disagree on how it works.
A signed direction from the President to federal agencies. It directs; regulations change only when agencies then act.
The yearly act of Congress on defense policy, where most changes to defense acquisition law are made. FY2026: Pub. L. 119-60.
The statute behind most of this guide, in Title 15 of the U.S. Code: the goals, the 8(a) program, SBIR and STTR.
Numbered blocks of contract text. FAR clauses begin 52, DFARS clauses 252; the digits after the point name the part they come from.

term: FAR Part 12 (commercial products and commercial services)
short: The FAR's rules for buying what the commercial market already sells, with simpler terms and fewer clauses.
The FAR part for negotiated purchases: a request for proposals, evaluation against stated factors, possible discussions, then award.
The FAR part on small business: representations, set-asides, the certified programs and subcontracting plans.

term: Market research and acquisition planning (FAR Parts 7 and 10)
short: The agency's homework before a purchase: who can meet the need, whether a commercial item will do, whether small firms can compete.
Competition open to all responsible firms. Set-asides limit it; a sole-source award skips it and normally needs a written justification.
SBA's governmentwide rulebook for SBIR and STTR. The posted version is from May 2023 and predates the 2026 act.
The defense instruction that sets up the Adaptive Acquisition Framework. Listed as DoWI 5000.02, April 2026; that text is unread here.
The governmentwide rulebook for grants and cooperative agreements: the counterpart of the FAR for financial assistance.

term: Certified cost or pricing data (Truth in Negotiations Act)
short: Cost facts a contractor must hand over and certify when a large contract is negotiated. $2.5 million in the FAR; $10 million in the defense statute.
Federal rules on how a contractor measures and assigns costs on large negotiated contracts. Small businesses are exempt.
The statute on how a contractor brings a claim against the Government. Only a party to the contract can use it.
The statute requiring bonds on federal construction, including a payment bond that protects unpaid subcontractors and suppliers.
The Government's own deadline for paying its prime: 30 days after a proper invoice or acceptance, with automatic interest when late.
Paying small businesses faster than 30 days. A prime paid early must pay its small subcontractors within 15 days.
A ban on equipment from five named Chinese telecommunications and video surveillance companies in federal contracting.

term: FASCSA orders (Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act)
short: Orders naming products or sources that contractors may not supply or use, on supply chain security grounds. Looked up in SAM.gov.
A prime's duty to report its first-tier subcontracts so the public can see them. Filed in SAM.gov since FSRS.gov retired on March 8, 2025.

term: ISR and SSR (subcontracting plan reports, formerly in eSRS)
short: The two reports a prime with a subcontracting plan files on its awards to small businesses. Filed in SAM.gov since eSRS retired in February 2026.

term: Service Contract Labor Standards (Service Contract Act)
short: Wage rules for federal service contracts over $2,500, with rates set by the Department of Labor.
The prevailing-wage rule for federal construction contracts above $2,000.

term: Buy American and the Trade Agreements Act (TAA)
short: The preference for domestic products in federal supply purchases, and the rule on which other countries' products may be offered on larger ones.
Two sets of rules: the State Department's ITAR for defense articles and the Commerce Department's EAR for civilian and dual-use items.
The government's system for confirming employment eligibility. Required by clause on contracts over $150,000 lasting 120 days or more.
The government's site for registering to do business with it, for posted contract opportunities and for award data. Registration is free.
The identifier the government uses for a firm in its award systems. Generated by SAM.gov; replaced the DUNS number on April 4, 2022.
An identifier for a business location, assigned by the Defense Logistics Agency. Needed before award above the micro-purchase threshold.
An industry classification number. The code assigned to a solicitation decides which size standard applies.
The statements a firm makes about itself (size, ownership, compliance) on which the Government relies. Most sit in the SAM record.
Past performance is a firm's record on earlier contracts; CPARS is the governmentwide system where agencies record it.
The DoD system holding a supplier's NIST SP 800-171 score and CMMC status. Reached through PIEE.
The DoD system for electronic invoices and receiving reports, reached through the PIEE portal.
The Treasury's electronic invoicing system used by civilian agencies, at no cost to vendors.
The government's database of contract awards. Its public search moved into SAM.gov; ezSearch was switched off on February 24, 2026.
The Treasury's public site showing where federal money goes, built from agency award data.
The governmentwide site where grant opportunities are posted and applications submitted.
The grants-side counterpart of a solicitation: the public notice that an agency has money to award and how to apply.
The defense department's portal for SBIR and STTR. All proposals to defense topics go through it.

term: SBIR.gov and the SBA Company Registry
short: SBA's site for SBIR and STTR. A firm registers there before proposing and receives an SBC Control ID.
SBA's listing of subcontracting opportunities posted by large contractors.
SBA's single application portal for 8(a), HUBZone, WOSB/EDWOSB and VOSB/SDVOSB certification. Applying is free.
SBA's certification program for veteran-owned and service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses, moved from VA on January 1, 2023.
The dollar line, $15,000 since October 1, 2025, below which an agency can buy with almost no formality, usually by purchase card.
The dollar line, $350,000 since October 1, 2025, up to which agencies use lighter procedures and reserve purchases for small business.
The FAR's quicker methods for smaller buys (Part 13), used up to $350,000, or up to $9 million for commercial products and services.
The public notice of a proposed contract action, posted on SAM.gov before the solicitation. Required above $25,000.
The federal budget year, October 1 to September 30, named for the year in which it ends. FY2027 began on October 1, 2026.

term: Size standard (what makes a firm small)
short: The ceiling, per industry, in employees or average annual receipts, under which a firm and its affiliates count as a small business concern.
The rule that decides whose employees and receipts are counted with a firm's own when its size is measured. It turns on control.
A subcontractor that is really doing the small prime's job on a set-aside. The finding makes the offeror ineligible as small.
Re-stating a firm's size and program status after award, within 30 days of a merger or sale and on contracts over five years.
A purchase reserved so that only small businesses, or only firms in one certified program, may compete for it.
A contract given to one firm without competition. For small firms it comes through the certified programs, each with a dollar ceiling.
The test for reserving a purchase for small business: can offers be expected from at least two capable small firms at fair prices?
SBA's nine-year, one-time business development program for small firms owned and controlled by disadvantaged individuals or certain entities.
The two tests an individual owner must meet for the 8(a) program. The social test changed on September 10, 2026.
A small business owned by an Indian Tribe, Alaska Native Corporation, Native Hawaiian Organization or Community Development Corporation.
SBA certification for small firms with a principal office in a HUBZone and at least 35% of employees living in one. Carries a 10 percent price preference.
A small firm at least 51% owned and controlled by women who are U.S. citizens. EDWOSB adds a personal financial ceiling. Set-asides exist only in designated industries.

term: Veteran-owned and service-disabled veteran-owned small business (VOSB, SDVOSB)
short: Small firms at least 51 percent owned and controlled by veterans (VOSB) or service-disabled veterans (SDVOSB), certified by SBA.
A status a firm claims for itself in good faith; there is no application. All current 8(a) participants qualify.
A firm that has held no DoD contract under full cost accounting standards coverage for at least a year. Nearly all small firms qualify.

term: Small business goals and the scorecard
short: The shares of federal contract dollars the law says should go to small firms (23 percent overall), and SBA's annual grade of each agency against them.
Challenges to another offeror's claim to be small, or to hold a program status. Due by the fifth business day after the apparent winner is announced.

term: SBA Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA)
short: The office inside SBA that hears appeals of size determinations, NAICS code designations and program status decisions.
The cap on how much of a set-aside contract a small prime may pass to firms that are not similarly situated: 50 percent for services.
A first-tier subcontractor with the same small business program status as the prime, and itself small.
Lets a small distributor or reseller win a supply set-aside if it supplies the product of a U.S. small-business manufacturer.
The contracting officer's finding, before any award, that a firm is able and fit to perform. Debarred or suspended firms are excluded.
The government official with authority to award and change a contract, and the one who decides whether a purchase is set aside.
An SBA representative who reviews a buying activity's planned purchases and recommends set-asides.
The SBA specialist on the subcontracting side, who reviews large primes' small business subcontracting programs.

term: OSDBU and OSBP (agency small business offices)
short: Each agency's in-house advocate for small business in its own purchases. Called the Office of Small Business Programs (OSBP) in DoD and NASA.
The person inside a large prime contractor who runs its small business subcontracting program: a small firm's first contact there.
The federal agency that writes the rules on who is small, runs the certification programs and oversees SBIR and STTR.
The agency that buys common goods and services for the rest of government and runs shared contracts and systems, including SAM.gov.
The office that decides bid protests and audits federal programs. Headed by the Comptroller General.
The research service of Congress. Its short reports explain programs and pending law; they describe the law and are not the law.
The defense department's internal auditor. Its 2021 audit examined other transactions awarded through consortia.

term: DCAA and the SF 1408 accounting survey
short: The defense agency that audits contractors' costs and accounting systems. It does not pre-approve systems; a survey against SF 1408 precedes a first cost-type award.
The determination that a company is eligible for access to classified information, granted by DCSA. A firm cannot apply for itself; it must be sponsored.
The FAR Council writes the FAR: the Office of Federal Procurement Policy (part of OMB) with DoD, GSA and NASA.
Local offices that help businesses sell to federal, state and local governments. Formerly Procurement Technical Assistance Centers.
Advising centers that give small firms individual help with capital, planning, technology, marketing and export.
A network of volunteer business mentors offering free mentoring, workshops and courses.
A national network of entrepreneurship centers offering free to low-cost counseling and training, including on federal contracts.
Centers serving service members, veterans, Guard and Reserve members and military spouses, under an SBA cooperative agreement.
The Commerce Department agency behind the MBDA Business Centers. Its status has been unsettled since a March 2025 executive order.
SBA's program funding state and regional organisations that help local firms compete for SBIR and STTR.

term: Department of War (DoW) / Department of Defense (DoD)
short: One department under two names. Department of War is the styling on its 2025-26 pages and memoranda; statutes and regulations still say Department of Defense.
The senior defense official in charge of a portfolio of related programs, created in 2025-26. Program managers report to the PAE.
The defense organisation that buys commercial technology through a commercial solutions opening and prototype other transactions.
The Department of the Air Force organisation that runs its SBIR and STTR topics; SpaceWERX does the same for the Space Force.
The Army's prize competitions, which can lead to SBIR or STTR awards and follow-on contracts.
A nonprofit innovation platform for U.S. Special Operations Command, running events, assessments, prize challenges and SBIR topics.
A defense marketplace of assessed five-minute pitch videos for AI, digital and data analytics products.
The health advanced research agency in HHS. It solicits through Innovative Solutions Openings and generally awards other transactions.
The HHS authority for medical countermeasures. It partners through a broad agency announcement, other transactions and consortia.
The Energy Department's advanced research agency. Its awards may be grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, prizes or other transactions.
The NIH office that has run governmentwide IT contracts, chiefly CIO-SP3. Its contracts are being wound down in 2026.
Agencies are usually named by their initials: NSF, NASA, NIH, HHS, DHS, DOE, DOT, USDA, EPA, NIST, NOAA, VA, FAA.
The federal program that pays small firms to research and develop their own technology, in phases. Only small firms may hold the awards.
SBIR's sibling for work done with a research institution: at least 40 percent by the small firm and 30 percent by the institution.
The first, small SBIR or STTR award: money to test whether an idea is feasible. Base guideline $150,000.
The main SBIR or STTR research and development award, continuing a Phase I. Base guideline $1,000,000.
Work that derives from, extends or completes earlier SBIR or STTR work, paid from other funds. It may be awarded sole source, with no dollar limit.
A Phase II awarded to a firm that never held the matching Phase I, on a written finding that feasibility is already shown.
One application covering Phase I and Phase II together, offered by NIH and NSF.
One additional Phase II award that continues the work of the first. Agencies give it their own names and terms.
A new tier for firms that already hold a Phase II: up to $30 million over 48 months, with 100 percent matching funds.
Extra money inside an SBIR or STTR award for commercialisation help: up to $6,500 in Phase I and $50,000 in Phase II.
Protection for the technical data a firm produces under an award: the Government may use it but not disclose it, for 20 years.
The Air Force's two programs that add matched money to a Phase II project to carry it toward Phase III.
The Army's program for scaling an SBIR technology with an Army customer and a prime integrator, matched 2:1:1.
Defense procurement money, $10 million to $50 million a project, for finished technology from small or nontraditional firms. Only government offices can request it.
A legally binding agreement that is not a procurement contract, grant or cooperative agreement. The FAR does not automatically apply.
An other transaction for basic, applied or advanced research. It expects cost sharing and carries no follow-on production authority.
An other transaction DoD uses to build and test a prototype. One of four conditions must hold, such as a nontraditional contractor taking a significant part.
The award that takes a successful prototype into production. It may go to the prototype's participants without further competition.
A standing membership group of firms through which an agency awards prototype projects in one technology area. Members usually pay dues.
The organisation that runs an OT consortium for the Government and passes project awards on to members.

term: Base agreement and project agreement (consortium OT)
short: The base agreement is the umbrella OT between the Government and a consortium; a project agreement is what a member signs with the manager to do the work.
A point in an other transaction at which the firm is paid a set amount for a defined result.
The part of a project's cost the firm pays itself. One third from non-Federal sources is one of four alternative conditions for a prototype OT.
A standing general solicitation: the agency posts problems, firms send short proposals, and the agency picks the solutions it wants.
An open call for research ideas, judged by peer or scientific review. It cannot be used to buy production.
An agreement to do joint research with a federal laboratory. The lab may give people, facilities and equipment, but no money.
An agreement between a federal laboratory and a go-between organisation that helps small businesses work with the lab.
NASA's instrument for partnerships, resting on its other transaction authority. Four types: nonreimbursable, reimbursable, funded, unfunded.
A contest in which an agency pays a reward for a result instead of buying work in advance. Challenge.gov, the old central listing, closed in March 2026.

term: Grant, cooperative agreement and procurement contract
short: The three standard instruments. A contract buys for the Government's own use; a grant or cooperative agreement supports a public purpose.
The defense department's six routes for buying a capability, each with its own instruction and clock.
The defense pathway for urgent operational needs, fielded in less than 2 years.
The defense pathway for getting a prototype, or a proven system, into the field within about five years.
The defense pathway for large, enduring military programs, run through phases and Milestones A, B and C.
The defense pathway for custom software: a first release within a year of funding, then deliveries at least annually.
The defense pathway for business software, with a commercial-first stance.
The defense pathway for contracted services at or above the simplified acquisition threshold.

term: Warfighting Acquisition System (and the Acquisition Transformation Strategy)
short: The name the defense department gave its reformed acquisition system in November 2025. The founding memorandum could not be read; the companion strategy was.
GSA's standing contract program for commercial products and services, also called the GSA Schedule. A contract there does not guarantee sales.
The category code for a group of products or services on the GSA Schedule.
The Schedule rule under which a contractor reports each sale's details to GSA monthly. Mandatory for all SINs since April 2026.
The fee a Schedule contractor pays GSA on its Schedule sales, currently 0.75%.
A large information technology contract that one agency awards to many firms and any agency may order from.
GSA's governmentwide contract program for non-IT services, with separate contracts for small business and each certified program.
GSA's small business GWAC for IT services, with Small Business, WOSB, HUBZone and SDVOSB pools.
GSA's unrestricted GWAC for information technology services, with no ceiling.
GSA's GWAC for IT services set aside for 8(a) firms, with a $50 billion ceiling.
GSA's GWAC for IT services set aside for service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses.
NASA's GWAC for IT, communications and audio-visual products and services. The sixth version, SEWP VI, starts on November 1, 2026.
A contract that sets terms for a period but not how much will be bought. The buying happens later, through orders, often among several holders.
An individual purchase placed under a larger standing contract: a task order for services, a delivery order for supplies.
A standing arrangement with a contractor to fill repetitive needs for supplies or services.
A contract that pays a set price for the work, whatever it costs the firm to perform.
A contract that pays the firm's allowable costs instead of a set price. It requires an adequate accounting system.
A contract that pays hourly labor rates plus the cost of materials. Allowed on commercial buys only with a documented justification.
An agency's advance list of contracts it expects to compete, published so firms can prepare. For planning only.
A notice asking firms that could do a job to identify themselves before any solicitation exists. Replies feed the set-aside decision.
An agency's early question to industry, used for planning before requirements are defined.
The synopsis announcing that a solicitation is coming, posted at least 15 days ahead outside commercial buys.
A single SAM.gov posting that both announces a commercial purchase and asks for offers.
The document in which an agency formally asks for offers: an RFQ for simpler buys, an RFP for larger ones.

term: SAM.gov notice types and set-aside codes
short: The labels on a SAM.gov contract opportunity: what kind of notice it is and which set-aside, if any, applies.
A one-page overview of what a firm can do: core competencies, past performance, differentiators and company data.
The agency's explanation to an unsuccessful offeror. It must be requested in writing within 3 days.

term: Bid protest (agency, GAO, Court of Federal Claims)
short: A formal challenge to a solicitation's terms or to an award, filed with the agency, with GAO ($500 fee, decision within 100 days) or in court.
The prime holds the contract with the Government. A subcontractor works for the prime or for another subcontractor and has no contract with the Government.
A large prime's written goals for subcontracting to small businesses, required on contracts over $900,000 ($2 million for construction).
A clause in the prime contract that the prime must repeat in its subcontracts.
A private agreement by which two or more firms pursue a contract together, usually as prime and subcontractor.
Two meanings: under FAR subpart 9.6, a joint venture or a prime with named subcontractors; on the GSA Schedule, a team of Schedule holders.
Two or more firms combining to bid and perform under a name of their own. It is small if each partner is small, or under an approved mentor-protégé pair.
A populated joint venture has its own staff doing the contract work; an unpopulated one performs through its partners' employees.
A joint venture generally may not win new contracts more than two years after its first award.
SBA's program letting a firm of any size mentor a small one. A joint venture of the pair counts as small where the protégé is small.
The defense department's own mentor-protégé program, under which mentors are reimbursed or credited for developing small suppliers.
The defense program for checking that contractors protect sensitive unclassified information. Its second phase was suspended on July 13, 2026.
Three tiers of required security: 15 basic requirements, the 110 of NIST SP 800-171, and 24 more. A C3PAO is an accredited outside assessor for Level 2.
The federal standard of 110 security requirements for protecting sensitive unclassified information on a contractor's own systems.

term: FCI and CUI (Federal contract information; controlled unclassified information)
short: Two classes of non-public information on a contractor's systems. FCI needs 15 basic safeguards; CUI needs NIST SP 800-171.
A commercial item sold in the market and supplied to the Government unchanged. Several requirements do not apply to COTS purchases.
Something sold in the commercial marketplace, not made only for the Government. Agencies must prefer it, and lighter rules apply.
